newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sets heavy calendar of 1997 privatizations.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sets heavy calendar of 1997 privatizations.

text.p: A flurry of sell-offs of government-owned railroads, airports, satellites, radio spectrum and ports should speed up Mexico's ambitious privatisation schedule in 1997, Mexican privatisation coordinator Jorge Silberstein told Reuters.

Since President Ernesto Zedillo took office two years ago, management of key ports, including Acapulco, Veracruz and Manzanillo, and most recently the key Northeast Railway trade route, have been auctioned to private companies.
The privatisation pace slowed in Zedillo's administration compared with the massive sales of banks, state-owned media and telecommunications assets under his predecessor.
"Last administration was primarily the privatisation of companies and this one is the privatisation of centres," Silberstein said.
"You have to create the whole legal framework that didn't exist. You have to create companies, divide equipment, do all the details."
With such preparation almost complete, Silberstein said next year will be a "hectic" one for privatisations.

In early 1997 the government plans to continue its rail track sell-off, with auctions for short lines scheduled for January or February, he said. Current concession owners will be allowed to bid for these short lines, but will not be permitted to own the larger units on the block later in the year to avoid creating a monopoly, Silberstein said.

The nation's 57 airports should begin to be sold in the second quarter of the year after guidelines for the sale are defined in the first quarter. Silberstein said no decision has been taken on whether to keep some airports in the state sector.

To continue with the piecemeal sale of the operating rights for the nation's ports, Silberstein said small multi-use port terminals will be auctioned in the first six months of 1997, followed by larger ports in the second half of the year.
"All of this depends on interest from investors, because sometimes we are ready and they are not," he said.
Still, foreign investors are almost entirely barred from leading bids for Mexican assets.
Mexican investment law allows only 49 percent foreign ownership in the privatisations. Exceptions can be granted through applications with the Commerce Ministry's foreign investment commission.
"To my knowledge, in the case of the Southeast (railroad), foreign investment will be limited to 49 percent. All the others, depending on the plans they present, can go above," Silberstein said.
Two of the five bidders for the Northeast Railway were eliminated because they were majority foreign-owned, Communications and Transport ministry officials said.
